what_its_for: Diclofenac is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) used to relieve pain, reduce swelling, and lower fever. It is commonly used for arthritis (including osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis), menstrual cramps, migraine headaches, muscle aches, and other types of mild to moderate pain.
how_to_take: Take diclofenac exactly as your doctor tells you. Swallow tablets or capsules whole with a full glass of water — do not crush, chew, or break them. You may take it with food or milk if it upsets your stomach. For the gel or patch form, apply it only to the skin area your doctor recommends. Wash your hands after applying the gel unless you are treating your hands. Do not cover the treated area with a tight bandage unless your doctor says to.
dosing: The dose depends on why you are taking it and what form you are using. A common adult dose for arthritis pain is 50 mg taken 2 to 3 times a day, or 75 mg taken twice a day. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions. Do not take more than prescribed, and do not take it for longer than recommended. Use the lowest dose that works for the shortest time possible.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store diclofenac tablets and capsules at room temperature, away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Keep it out of the bathroom medicine cabinet. Store the gel or patch at room temperature and keep the patch in its sealed pouch until you are ready to use it. Keep all forms of this medicine out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medicine down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about a medicine take-back program.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking diclofenac, as it increases the risk of stomach bleeding. Do not take other NSAIDs (such as ibuprofen or naproxen) at the same time unless your doctor approves. Avoid prolonged sun exposure or tanning beds if using the gel or patch. Do not use the patch near heat sources like heating pads. Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery if this medicine makes you feel dizzy or drowsy. Do not take aspirin for pain relief while on this medication unless your doctor tells you to.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you notice: black, tarry, or bloody stools; vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds; chest pain or shortness of breath; sudden weakness on one side of the face or body; slurred speech; severe stomach pain; swelling of your hands, feet, or ankles; yellowing of your skin or eyes (jaundice); dark urine; or a severe skin rash with blistering or peeling. Also call your doctor if your pain gets worse or does not improve after a few days.
when_it_works: You may start to feel some pain relief within 30 minutes to a few hours after taking a dose. However, for ongoing conditions like arthritis, it may take 1 to 2 weeks of regular use before you notice the full benefit. Do not stop taking it early just because you feel better — continue as directed by your doctor.
special_populations: Older adults (65 years and older) are at higher risk for stomach bleeding, kidney problems, and heart-related side effects and should use the lowest effective dose. Pregnant women should avoid diclofenac, especially during the last 3 months of pregnancy, as it can harm the unborn baby. Breastfeeding mothers should talk to their doctor before using it. Children should only use diclofenac if a doctor specifically prescribes it. People with heart disease, high blood pressure, kidney disease, liver disease, or a history of stomach ulcers should use this medicine with extra caution and close medical supervision.
